articles.title: Explosive-laden truck rams into mosque near police offices in Pakistan's Kohat; 16 dead
articles.summary: Pakistan News: At least 16 people were killed and more than 56 injured in a suicide explosion at a mosque inside the Kohat Police Lines in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunk.
articles.body: At least 16 people were killed and more than 56 injured in a suicide explosion at a mosque inside the Kohat Police Lines in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Friday, officials said.The explosion occured in Kohat, a district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, near the Afghanistan border, during Friday prayers, bringing down part of the building and prompting a major rescue operation. Emergency teams and local residents searched through the rubble for survivors, while at least two armed gunmen tried to enter the police compound and exchanged fire with officers, police told AP.According to Dawn, Rescue 1122 Khyber Pakhtunkhwa spokesperson Bilal Ahmed Faizi said emergency teams rushed to the site after receiving information about the explosion and began rescue operations.The injured were taken to nearby hospitals for treatment, while roads leading to the blast site were closed, Geo News reported. Rescue teams remained at the scene to assess the situation.The location was initially described by rescue officials as being near the Old Police Lines. However, a statement from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa inspector general Zulfiqar Hameed said the explosion occurred at a mosque inside the Police Lines complex.“Following the explosion, an exchange of fire ensued with the armed terrorists,” the statement said. Hameed also directed officials to ensure the best possible medical treatment for those injured in the blast.Separately, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa chief minister Sohail Afridi and governor Faisal Karim Kundi condemned the explosion and expressed solidarity with those affected. The blast comes a day after a roadside bomb targeted a security forces convoy in northwestern Hangu district, killing six soldiers. Separately, government forces carried out raids in several areas on Thursday and killed 10 militants suspected to be affiliated with the Pakistani Taliban, according to the military and local police.Footage circulating on social media showed the roof of the mosque had collapsed. Rescuers and local residents could be seen pulling injured people from the rubble and carrying them to ambulances.No group had immediately claimed responsibility for the explosion. Suspicion could nevertheless fall on the Pakistani Taliban, or Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which has carried out repeated attacks against security personnel and civilians in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, AP said.In 2023, a suicide bombing at a mosque in Peshawar, the provincial capital, killed 101 people. The TTP is separate from Afghanistan's Taliban but maintains an alliance with the group.Pakistan has repeatedly accused the Taliban government in Kabul of providing shelter to TTP members and allowing cross-border attacks to be carried out from Afghan territory. Kabul has denied the allegations.Authorities have yet to establish the precise nature of Friday's explosion or identify those responsible. Further details are expected as investigators assess the scene and the condition of those injured.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 1981, a Florida sinkhole grew overnight to roughly 300 feet wide, swallowing a three-bedroom home, five Porsches, a pickup and a swimming pool
articles.summary: US News: In May 1981, a dramatic sinkhole in Winter Park, Florida, grew to 300 feet wide overnight, consuming a home, luxury cars, and turning the area into a lake known as Lake Rose. Explore the geological causes and aftermath of this eye-opening event.
articles.body: On an ordinary evening in Winter Park, Florida, the ground began to give way without warning. What began as a small depression near a home soon became one of Florida's most dramatic sinkhole collapses. Over the following hours, the opening spread beneath homes, roads and nearby buildings, turning a familiar neighbourhood into the edge of a rapidly expanding crater.According to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), the sinkhole first appeared on the evening of May 8, 1981, near the intersection of South Denning Drive and West Fairbanks Avenue. By the following day, it had reached about 300 feet in diameter, with a visible depth of roughly 80 feet in one of the USGS observations. The collapse swallowed a house, undermined an automotive repair shop and consumed part of a community swimming pool. Several Porsche cars from the repair shop were also pulled into the hole.When the ground began to disappearThe cave-in occurred rather rapidly. An opening formed on May 8, started to expand during the night, and then started to expand faster on the next morning. According to a later USGS investigation, the opening grew from about 40 feet wide at first to roughly 80 feet overnight, then rapidly to about 300 feet between late morning and noon on May 9. It is thought that such rapid expansion was caused by the roof collapse of an underground cavity.The collapse did not remain confined to one property. A three-bedroom house was consumed in the widening hole, and parts of nearby roads and buildings were at risk. The municipal swimming pool became a part of the collapsing process as well. USGS photographs taken during this phenomenon illustrate the breaking of the pool and water flowing into the sinkhole.The submerged cars became some of the most recognisable features of the collapse. Five Porsches owned by an automobile company in the area were engulfed when the earth under the land subsided. Evidence suggests that a pickup truck or recreational vehicle was also lost in the collapse. The cars were eventually recovered, but some were still trapped in the new opening created. No one died in the incident. The owners of the house that was in danger escaped the collapsing building.What was happening beneath Winter Park?The surface collapse resulted from processes deep below the ground. Central Florida lies on soluble rocks of limestone and dolostone. As water moves through the rocks, it can dissolve material and form cavities beneath the surface. Eventually, when the weight on the cavity becomes too much, there is likely to be a collapse.According to research published in The Science of the Total Environment, cover-collapse and cover-suffosion sinkholes are widespread in central Florida's karst terrain. The study found that factors including groundwater movement, rainfall and differences in groundwater levels can influence when sinkholes develop. It also identified rapid changes in groundwater conditions as important factors in the timing of some collapses.The Winter Park case shows how quickly a geological process can affect the surface. According to USGS findings, the collapse was linked to the deeper Floridan aquifer. Initially, the water level in the sinkhole was deeper than 80 feet beneath the ground level. Later, when debris fell into the hole, the water level began to increase due to partial blocking of the connection with the deeper aquifer.From giant crater to Lake RoseAfter the most catastrophic part of the sinkhole event, it continued to change. As debris accumulated underground, water began to collect in the hole. According to the USGS report, the water level kept increasing throughout the next weeks and months until it reached a certain level just a few feet above the surface. Later, the city was able to stabilise the area by filling parts of the hole with debris. The hole eventually became a permanent lake. This lake became known as Lake Rose, named after Mae Rose Williams, who lost her house in this event.The final dimensions vary slightly between historical accounts and scientific observations. USGS records describe the sinkhole at around 300 feet across during the most active phase, while later measurements put the feature at approximately 350 feet wide. The USGS's Floridan Aquifer System study identifies it as a 350-foot-wide, 75-foot-deep cover-collapse sinkhole.Today, the site looks very different from the sinkhole that startled Winter Park in 1981. Houses, cars, pools, and even stretches of road fell victim to this event within just a few hours, but the underlying process of sinkhole formation has been ongoing for much longer. The event is a clear example of how Florida’s geology can alter the surface in a very short time. The Winter Park sinkhole later became a lake and remains a striking part of the city's history.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 14 years after he vanished, a shocking betrayal may reveal what happened to US journalist Austin Tice
articles.summary: US News: He was 31 and had just celebrated his birthday a few days ago while listening to Taylor Swift songs, before heading to Lebanon as an independent freel.
articles.body: He was 31 and had just celebrated his birthday a few days ago while listening to Taylor Swift songs, before heading to Lebanon as an independent freelance journalist and photographer covering the ongoing Syrian civil war. That was the last time the former US Marine and Georgetown University law student was seen out and about. About 14 years later, his disappearance still remains a mystery.A new BBC investigation published on September 17 has revealed yet another update in the case. According to the report, Tice was betrayed by his driver, an alleged informant for the Assad regime and kidnapped.Who was Austin Tice?Tice, a Houston native, served in the Marine from 2005 to 2011 and returned to the Middle East as a journalist. At the time, he was covering the Syrian civil war. During his time there, he filed reports for major news organisations including The Washington Post, CBS News and McClatchy. He aimed to document the conflict firsthand and was attempting to travel to Beirut, Lebanon, when he disappeared near a checkpoint in Daraya, Syria, on August 13, 2012.Following his kidnapping, a video surfaced a month later of a blindfolded Tice being held by armed men saying, "Oh Jesus." That was the last time anyone heard from him, according to The Guardian. In 2022, then-President Joe Biden said “with certainty” that the U.S. knew that Syrian authorities had Tice in their possession.The Assad regime previously denied all allegations of kidnapping the American journalist. As the regime fell 12 years later, tens of thousands of people emerged from the administration's prisons, yet Tice was not one of them. Following the regime’s collapse in 2024, the BBC uncovered confidential Syrian intelligence files on Tice, which indicated he was detained by now-former Syrian President Bashar al-Assad’s government.What happened to Austin Tice?The British outlet added that it spoke with Abu Ali, a former member of the National Defence Forces (NDF), a militia loyal to Assad. Abu Ali said that Tice’s driver, whom sources allege passed information to the regime, told an NDF official that Tice had been going through rebel areas and reporting on the opposition.At the time, the Assad government was cracking down on journalists reporting on its human rights abuses. The intelligence about Tice went all the way up to Assad himself, whom Ali says told the group to abduct the journalist. NDF surveillance on Tice continued after Assad’s alleged request, the BBC reported, until the driver reported to the militia that Tice’s actions appeared suspicious, said Abu Ali.When it was time for Tice to leave Syria after he celebrated his 31st birthday on August 11, 2012, he was planning to take a break in Lebanon. However, he was driven to a state facility where an NDF official had an office on the outskirts of Damascus, according to sources.Abu Ali later said the driver told him that he pulled out a gun as the car approached the gates, the BBC reported. At first, Tice thought his driver was joking until he realised what was happening. Abu Ali also recounted that Tice pulled out his chequebook and offered the driver any amount of money instead of going ahead with the abduction. Instead, NDF officials took Tice and covered his eyes, according to Abu Ali.BBC also reported that the driver's name was Hamid Abu Obeid and his family did not know his current whereabouts and said they were unaware of his alleged involvement in Tice's disappearance. The family, who live in poverty as Palestinian refugees, said Abu Obeid was offered a passport, Syrian citizenship and a weapon if he turned in Tice. They claimed that Abu Obeid only got a pistol after the kidnapping, the BBC reported.Abu Obeid’s wife told the outlet that her husband disappeared after a man who knew about his role in Tice’s case threatened to inform the US embassy in return for a promise of asylum. He took some money, told his wife he was going shopping, and she said she has not seen him since. She does not know if he is in hiding, or if he has been detained or killed. The wife said that after Abu Obeid vanished, masked men came by their house and took away his laptop and other belongings.Still looking for Austin TiceIn December 2024, Debra Tice, Austin's mother, spoke at the National Press Club in Washington, D.C., and claimed her son is alive based on a then-new report. “We have a significant source that has already been vetted all over our government; Austin Tice is alive, Austin Tice is treated well,” Debra said at the press conference. “And there is no doubt about that.”Debra previously expressed optimism that President Donald Trump would bring her son home after she said Trump previously “had an obsession” with helping Austin during his first term. As of now, the US government maintains an active investigation into Tice and offers a multi-million-dollar reward for information that leads to his safe return.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1997, scientists released captive-bred bilbies on an Australian island; 10 years later, they had occupied the entire island
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In 1997, conservationists introduced captive-bred greater bilbies to Thistle Island in South Australia, a place the species had never historically inh.
articles.body: In 1997, conservationists introduced captive-bred greater bilbies to Thistle Island in South Australia, a place the species had never historically inhabited. The release was part of a wider national effort to protect the vulnerable marsupial from introduced predators such as foxes and feral cats. According to the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water, Government of Australia’s Recovery Plan for the Greater Bilby, surveys carried out roughly a decade later found the population had grown and spread across the entire island. Here's what the plan reveals about this and related reintroduction efforts, along with where things stand today.How captive-bred bilbies colonised the entire Thistle IslandThistle Island, off South Australia's coast, had no historical bilby population before captive-bred animals were released there in 1997. Because the island lacked mainland predators such as foxes and feral cats, the bilbies could establish themselves without the predation pressure that limits mainland populations. Surveys undertaken roughly a decade after the release, cited in the recovery plan as Berris et al. (2019), found that the population had increased and occupied the entire island. The plan holds this up as an example of how predator-free islands can support successful bilby introductions well outside the species' former range.128 reintroduced bilbies and their spread across Western AustraliaA comparable reintroduction unfolded at Matuwa, a 2,500 square kilometre area in Western Australia jointly managed by the Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions and Martu Indigenous rangers since 2000. Feral cats have been controlled there through annual baiting and trapping since 2004, and the area is fenced to exclude camels and domestic stock. Between 2007 and 2009, 128 bilbies were reintroduced to Matuwa. Since then, the population has spread throughout most of the intensively managed area and has also colonised adjacent land, showing that sustained predator control can support bilby recovery even outside a fenced enclosure.Other sites and the wider bilby reintroduction networkBeyond islands and unfenced managed areas like Matuwa, the greater bilby has been reintroduced to large fenced enclosures across its former range, including Mallee Cliffs National Park, Arid Recovery Reserve, Francois Peron National Park, Scotia Sanctuary, Yookamurra Sanctuary, Mt Gibson Sanctuary, Currawinya National Park, Pilliga State Conservation Area, Sturt National Park and Newhaven Sanctuary. These enclosures, some covering up to 262,000 hectares, exclude introduced predators while still exposing bilbies to natural selection pressures. The combined population across these reintroduced sites is estimated at around 3,000 individuals, helping to restore ecological processes such as soil turnover and maintain genetic diversity across the species' range.Why the greater bilby is still listed as vulnerable, and how it's faring nowDespite successes at Thistle Island and Matuwa, the greater bilby remains listed as vulnerable under the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999. Its range has contracted by more than 80 per cent since European settlement, and the species survives largely in the Northern Territory, northern Western Australia, and small, isolated Queensland populations. Predation by foxes and feral cats remains the most significant ongoing threat, alongside habitat loss, altered fire regimes and reduced Traditional Owner land management.A more recent ecological study ‘Digging deeper: habitat selection within the home ranges of a threatened marsupial’ on Thistle Island's temperate-climate population has since recorded densities as high as 101 bilbies per square kilometre, far above the 0 to 0.2 bilbies per square kilometre typical of arid-zone populations, indicating the island population has stayed well established. More broadly, the Australian Wildlife Conservancy's latest annual bilby census across its protected sanctuaries in Western Australia, the Northern Territory, South Australia and New South Wales put the total population at 5,330 individuals, an increase of around 2,000 animals on the previous year and more than four times the number recorded in 2021. Together, these findings suggest the wider reintroduction effort is continuing to build momentum even as the species remains formally vulnerable.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Pentagon weighs withdrawing 25,000-40,000 troops from Europe: Report
articles.summary: Europe News: The Pentagon is considering withdrawing at least 25,000 US troops from Europe, potentially cutting the American military presence on the continent by .
articles.body: The Pentagon is considering withdrawing at least 25,000 US troops from Europe, potentially cutting the American military presence on the continent by nearly one-third, NBC News reported Thursday.The drawdown could be even larger, with some options involving the withdrawal of as many as 40,000 troops, according to current and former US and Western officials cited by NBC. Around 80,000 US troops are currently stationed in Europe.No final decision has been made on the possible reductions.Germany, Italy and Spain, which host some of the largest US military deployments in Europe, are among the countries that could be affected.Pentagon reviewing US military presence in EuropeThe options are part of a six-month Pentagon review of the US military presence in Europe. General Alexus Grynkewich, who heads US European Command and serves as NATO's supreme allied commander, is expected to submit an initial assessment to defence secretary Pete Hegseth on Friday.The review is expected to outline several options involving US aviation, naval and ground forces. It could also consider moving some American troops within Europe, including towards NATO's eastern flank.Hegseth is expected to receive a final recommendation on November 6, after which any proposal would be presented to President Donald Trump. Any troop withdrawal would take place only after that process.European allies concerned over possible drawdownThe Trump administration has argued that European countries should take greater responsibility for their conventional defence, while the US shifts more military resources towards other regions and priorities.The prospect of a major reduction has raised concerns among some US lawmakers and European governments, who have warned that a rapid withdrawal could affect NATO's ability to deter Russia.NBC also reported that the State Department and Pentagon have differed over the review. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly intervened in June after the Pentagon prepared to brief NATO defence ministers on potential large-scale reductions.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Maryland is planning a replacement for the Chesapeake Bay Bridge; farmers now want millions set aside because the new crossing could accelerate development and permanently remove Eastern Shore farmland
articles.summary: US News: Maryland's plan to replace the Chesapeake Bay Bridge is raising concerns among farmers and conservation groups on the state's Eastern Shore. They say .
articles.body: Maryland's plan to replace the Chesapeake Bay Bridge is raising concerns among farmers and conservation groups on the state's Eastern Shore. They say the new crossing could increase development pressure on farmland and other open land, and are asking the state to create a dedicated fund to preserve agricultural areas.The Maryland Transportation Authority Board voted in December to move ahead with a plan to build two new four-lane spans across the Chesapeake Bay and remove the existing bridges. WBOC reported. The project would also widen Routes 50 and 301 to eight lanes, with four lanes in each direction. It could also include a shared-use path for cyclists and pedestrians.The new spans would have full shoulders and greater clearance underneath, allowing larger ships to pass through. The project is still several years away, with final design expected to begin in 2028 and construction targeted for 2032.As the plans move forward, the Eastern Shore Land Conservancy is working with local governments and conservation groups on a proposal for a land preservation fund linked to the bridge project. Queen Anne's, Caroline and Talbot counties have signed a letter supporting the idea.Development pressure on Eastern ShoreAn MTA report on the Bay Crossing project found that more than 111,000 acres across the Eastern Shore are vulnerable to growth and development pressure. The land includes farms, forests and waterways in Caroline, Queen Anne's and Talbot counties. The three counties together account for about 22% of Maryland's agricultural sales, according to the report.Jay Falstad, executive director of the Queen Anne's Conservation Association, said, "The goal is to try and protect farmland for the future," Falstad said. "Queen Anne's County is an agricultural gem, and you would not want to see that disrupted with a sea of subdivision development that would follow in the wake of a new Bay bridge."Falstad said most of the proposed funding would likely go to Queen Anne's and Caroline counties, which he said are the state's largest grain-producing counties.“Right now it's a request of the state basically saying that if you're going to spend a few billion dollars on a new Bay bridge, then you ought to be prepared to allocate a few hundred million dollars for land preservation,” Falstad said.He also said agriculture is Queen Anne's County's top economic sector and that the county has preserved nearly 40% of its farmland. Falstad remains opposed to the bridge project, saying the state has not adequately justified the need for a new span given the remaining lifespan of the existing bridge.Conservation group proposes land fundCarol Bean, land use and policy manager for the Eastern Shore Land Conservancy, said the preservation fund is still only a concept. No formal agreement is in place, and discussions are continuing with the Maryland Department of Transportation and other state agencies.Bean said the group is trying to align its work with the formal record of decision for the bridge project, which she said could come as early as this fall or early winter."The state has made the decision. They've picked a route. They're moving ahead with it," Bean said. "So in our perspective, it's how do you do that in the most responsible way that respects the kind of tradition and economy of the Eastern Shore. And land preservation is a really key way that you can do that. It's a way you can protect the investment in the bridge as well."Bean said development along the corridor could also affect the bridge's purpose of easing traffic. "If you don't protect that corridor, you end up with more development, which means more access points," she said. "You can use land preservation as a strategic tool to protect that investment, but also to fundamentally support these key industries of the Eastern Shore, like agriculture."Caroline County watches developmentTravis Breeding, president of the Caroline County Board of Commissioners, said the county wants to protect its rural character as development pressure grows."The rural heritage of Caroline County is very important to us, and we want to preserve that," Breeding said. "The additional expansion of the Bay bridge could increase development here in Caroline County, and we really want to slow that down."Breeding said the proposed fund remains a concept. The request is for the Maryland Department of Transportation and the Transportation Authority to establish a funding stream to preserve agricultural land in the Mid-Shore region.Farmers want a sayStephen Kraszewski, a Queen Anne's County farmer whose family runs Mason Farms Produce on a fifth-generation farm, said farming is closely tied to the region's rural way of life. He said Queen Anne's County has more corn and soybean farmland than any other county in Maryland."It feels like there's a target on our back," Kraszewski said, noting that the bridge route runs through Kent Island and directly through the county on the way to beach destinations including Ocean City, Rehoboth and Lewes. "Those farmers, they want to see their way of life preserved, just not taken over. Not bulldozed. Not removed."Kraszewski said losing farmland could affect the wider farming community. "If losing farmland means you lose a farmer, you lose some of the heritage that's already here," he said. "We are a community. We try to work with each other. We talk to each other. We solve problems together. And one less farmer is a real blow to our community."He said he is not against growth but wants farmers to have a role in decisions about development. "We want structured expansion, with everybody's input, not just simple meetings that record people saying what they want, and then they're tossed aside," he said. "We want a voice, and we want to have our input in how it all works out .We want to make sure people have healthy food to eat and local food. That's probably the most important thing that you can have for anybody who enjoys those three meals a day is local, healthy produce. And yeah, you have to have land to grow that,” Kraszewski added.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Watch: Hundreds of thousands rally in Iran as volunteers pledge to defend country, military hardware on display
articles.summary: Middle East News: Hundreds of thousands of Iranians rallied in Tehran on Friday in a government-organised show of defiance, with volunteers pledging to undergo military.
articles.body: Hundreds of thousands of Iranians rallied in Tehran on Friday in a government-organised show of defiance, with volunteers pledging to undergo military training and defend the country amid the ongoing war and mounting economic pressure.The rally was the largest such government-backed demonstration since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February, according to The Associated Press. Iran's leadership used the event to project national unity while the country faces worsening economic conditions under a US naval blockade of Iranian ports and new sanctions.The demonstration also marked the public launch of a campaign called “Janfaday-e Iran”, or the “ones who sacrifice their lives for Iran”. Volunteers marched through central Tehran in combat uniforms carrying Iranian flags, while crowds cheered them.Iran's Revolutionary Guard chief in Tehran, Gen Hassan Hassanzadeh, said more than 600,000 people had registered for the programme, with more than 1 million expected to undergo training. Iran's state broadcaster estimated that more than 300,000 people were on the streets on Friday morning.The volunteers are expected to receive basic military training, including training with assault rifles. They would serve as an additional layer of security alongside Iran's powerful Revolutionary Guard and its volunteer Basij force.Basij chief Hossein Taeb said at the rally that the volunteers would be prepared for “full-fledged defense” and that similar rallies would soon be held in other Iranian cities.Taeb also said the new trainees would become a “nightmare” for Iran's enemies. President Masoud Pezeshkian, military commanders and other senior officials attended the event.Some participants trampled on US and Israeli flags, while crowds chanted “Death to America” and “Death to Israel.”“I am here to tell (US President Donald) Trump that we Iranians have no fear about his threats against our homeland,” said Marzieh Afaghi, 24, who attended the rally with her toddler and husband. “No one in history could invade Iran and remain there.”Iran displays military hardwareThe rally also provided Iran an opportunity to display military equipment, including anti-aircraft systems and drones.Female Revolutionary Guard members wearing black headscarves were seen sitting alongside truck-mounted machine guns, while the Guard displayed drones that have been used extensively against ships in the Strait of Hormuz.Iran has asserted control over the strategic waterway since the war began, disrupting the movement of oil and natural gas shipments from the Gulf region.Volunteers could also strengthen internal securityBeyond the war effort, Friday's mobilisation could give Iran's hardline leadership another organised force to respond to future domestic unrest.Iran witnessed some of its largest nationwide protests in January, shortly before the war began. The demonstrations initially focused on economic difficulties before expanding into broader opposition to the country's theocratic system.Activists have claimed that a subsequent crackdown killed more than 7,000 people and resulted in tens of thousands of arrests. Those figures have not been independently verified by The Associated Press.In May, Iranian officials said more than 30 million people, in a country of about 90 million, had volunteered through online forms or public gatherings to sacrifice their lives for the country's leadership. The Associated Press said it could not independently verify that figure.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: From H-1B to green cards: Why Indian tech workers are facing a double squeeze in the US
articles.summary: US News: For years, the H-1B visa was the front door, and the green card was the destination. Indian technology professionals accepted the lottery odds, years .
articles.body: For years, the H-1B visa was the front door, and the green card was the destination. Indian technology professionals accepted the lottery odds, years in limbo and uncertainty because the pathway, however slow, was open. Now, both ends of that pathway are under pressure.With nearly 10 lakh Indians already in the US employment-based green-card backlog, the journey from temporary worker to permanent resident is becoming a two-sided squeeze: getting in is harder, while getting out of the visa queue can take decades.On September 8, US Department of Labor Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito announced that Cognizant's new PERM filings had been suspended amid an investigation into alleged fraud and misuse of employment-based visa programmes.Days later, he said the same had happened to Cloudera. The department has not publicly disclosed the number of employees affected, the duration of the suspensions or detailed allegations against either company.Rajiv Dabhadkar, founder of the National Organisation for Software and Technology Professionals (NOSTOPS), told TOI,“Cognizant's PERM suspension sends a broader signal to employers and employees: immigration policy and sponsorship practices are no longer just HR considerations; they are becoming central to long-term workforce planning.”But the bigger story goes beyond one company. Indian professionals are caught between tighter scrutiny of temporary work visas and a permanent residency system where the wait for a green card is already extraordinarily long.Put together, these two trends describe something more specific than “tighter immigration policy”: they describe a double squeeze, a narrowing gate to enter the system and a barely moving line to exit it.What a PERM suspension actually changes, and what it doesn’tPERM, or Program Electronic Review Management, is generally the labour-certification stage in which a US employer seeks Department of Labor approval to sponsor a foreign worker for permanent residence.It is not the green card itself.Typical employer-sponsored green-card routeH-1B visa → Work in the USPERM → Employer starts the labour-certification processI-140 → Employer files the immigrant petitionPriority date → Worker waits for the date to become currentI-485 / Consular processing → Apply for permanent residenceGreen card → Permanent residency is grantedThat means a suspension of new PERM filings can prevent an employer from moving new workers into the permanent-residency process. It does not automatically mean that every existing H-1B worker's visa or previously approved immigration case has been cancelled.That distinction matters because Cognizant's development has created anxiety among Indian workers who may already be planning their careers around employer-sponsored permanent residence.But Cognizant's PERM suspension does not by itself explain why Indian workers face such a difficult green-card journey. That problem existed long before the latest investigation.Dabhadkar said, “For Indian tech professionals, the emerging lesson is that a US job may be a career opportunity, but a US green card is a separate and increasingly uncertain proposition.”The first squeeze: staying on H-1BFor many Indian technology workers, the H-1B is the entry point into a longer US career.The visa allows US employers to employ foreign workers in specialised occupations, including many technology roles. The system has an annual cap of 85,000 new H-1B visas: 65,000 under the regular quota and another 20,000 for foreign graduates with advanced degrees from US universities.Demand has long exceeded supply, making the selection process highly competitive.But the bigger issue for workers already in the US is that H-1B status is tied to employment. If an employee loses the job, immigration status can quickly become a problem.That risk could become even greater if a new proposal from the Department of Homeland Security is finalised.DHS has proposed removing the current discretionary 60-day grace period that allows certain H-1B and other employment-visa holders to remain in the US after their jobs end while looking for another employer or immigration option. The proposal is still subject to the rule-making process and is not current law.For an Indian worker who has spent years building a career in the US, that could turn a routine job change into an immigration emergency.The second squeeze is much bigger: the green-card queueThis is where India's immigration problem becomes very different from that of many other nationalities.The US limits employment-based immigrant visas and also applies a statutory per-country limit. India has far more applicants in employment-based categories than the available annual numbers can accommodate.The result is a massive backlog.A recent National Foundation for American Policy analysis estimated that nearly 1 million Indians are stuck in the US employment-based green-card backlog, accounting for nearly 79 per cent of the estimated 1.26 million people waiting in the first three employment-based categories.For some applicants, the projected wait is extraordinarily long. NFAP has estimated that an Indian professional entering the queue in 2026 could face a potential wait of 179 years in EB-2 and 38 years in EB-3, under its modelling assumptions.These are NFAP projections, not official government wait times, and actual waits can change with demand, visa availability and changes to US law.But what does a 179-year wait mean for a 22-year-old’s idea of the future? Dabhadkar said, “The precise number is almost beside the point. What matters is the mismatch between the time horizon of immigration and the time horizon of a human life.”And that raises a question far larger than immigration: What happens to the American Dream after the American degree?For September 2026, the State Department lists India's EB-2 category as unavailable for final action, while the EB-3 final action date is January 1, 2014 and EB-1 is October 15, 2022.These dates determine whether a worker who has completed years of employment and employer sponsorship can actually receive permanent residence.The State Department has also said all available FY2026 EB-2 immigrant visas for India had been used.Why does India have such a huge queue?The basic problem is a mismatch between how many Indians seek employment-based permanent residence and how many visas are available under US law.India produces a large pool of engineers, software professionals and other highly skilled workers who seek jobs in the US. Many enter through the H-1B system and later seek employment-based green cards.But employment-based immigration numbers are limited.The State Department says the worldwide employment-based preference limit for FY2026 is 186,317, while the per-country limit is set at 7 per cent of the combined family-sponsored and employment-based preference limits, subject to statutory rules and exceptions.India is one of the countries whose applicants are oversubscribed. That creates a peculiar situation.An Indian engineer can have a highly paid job, an advanced degree, a US employer willing to sponsor a green card and years of tax and employment history in America, yet still have to wait for a visa number to become available.What happens to a worker caught in the middle?For an Indian technology professional, getting an H-1B is just the beginning. The worker may spend years changing employers, extending H-1B status and waiting for an employer to start and progress a green-card application.That dependence can create another layer of uncertainty. A delay in PERM can push back the green-card process, while an employer ending sponsorship can force the worker to explore another immigration route. Even after reaching later stages, the Indian priority-date backlog can keep permanent residence out of reach.The result is two timelines moving at different speeds: temporary status depends on continued employment, while permanent residence can remain years away.The pressure is spreading beyond green cardsThe green-card queue is only one part of the squeeze. The H-1B system itself is facing a more restrictive environment.The administration has pursued higher costs, greater scrutiny and changes to employment-visa rules.At the same time, Indian IT companies have already been reducing their dependence on new H-1B workers.An NFAP analysis of USCIS data found that seven major Indian-based IT companies received 4,573 approvals for H-1B petitions for initial employment in FY2025, down 37 per cent from FY2024 and 70 per cent from 2015.Cognizant's own figure in that analysis fell sharply, from 2,873 approvals for initial employment in FY2024 to 743 in FY2025.The decline does not mean Indian IT companies no longer need H-1B workers. Rather, companies have increasingly relied on local US hiring, offshore delivery and other locations to reduce dependence on moving workers through the H-1B system.For individual Indian professionals, however, that shift offers little comfort if they are already in the US and waiting for permanent residence.From temporary worker to permanent resident: where is the exit?That is the central question facing many Indian technology workers.The US remains one of the world's biggest technology markets, and companies continue to need skilled professionals. But for an Indian worker, getting into the US labour market and securing permanent residency are increasingly separate challenges.H-1B can get the worker into the US. It does not guarantee a green card.PERM can start the employer-sponsored permanent-residency process. It does not guarantee a green card.And even an approved immigrant petition does not necessarily mean an Indian applicant can immediately become a permanent resident, because the priority-date backlog can remain.It shows how a worker's path to permanent residence can be affected by employer-level immigration scrutiny even before the worker reaches the already crowded green-card queue.For Indian tech workers, that is the real double squeeze: the rules governing the temporary route are becoming more uncertain at the same time that the permanent route remains heavily backlogged.The result is a rising group of highly skilled professionals who may have lived, worked and built careers in America for years, yet still cannot say when the temporary chapter of their immigration journey will finally end.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: California approves $42 million to acquire 2,060-acre Wild Cherry Canyon; after 25+ years of conservation efforts, the move would permanently remove the threat of residential development
articles.summary: US News: After more than two decades of efforts, California approved a $42 million grant to permanently conserve Wild Cherry Canyon, a 2,060-acre stretch of co.
articles.body: After more than two decades of efforts, California approved a $42 million grant to permanently conserve Wild Cherry Canyon, a 2,060-acre stretch of coastal hills in San Luis Obispo County. The California State Coastal Conservancy has authorised the grant to acquire both the property’s leasehold interest and underlying fee title in two transactions, with the first closing by year’s end and the second anticipated by mid-2027.The land, which overlooks Avila Beach and sits within the broader 12,000-acre Diablo Canyon Lands, had remained vulnerable for decades under a long-term private lease, with the risk of residential development. The grant will help remove the threat of future development and eventually turn the property into a permanently protected nature preserve.“This has been 25 years in the making,” Senator John Laird said in a release. “I worked to protect Wild Cherry Canyon as California’s Natural Resources Secretary, and many others worked on it before and since. There were plenty of times when it looked like it might not happen, but the Central Coast community never gave up. Today, we can finally celebrate a major victory for this incredible piece of our coastline.”The outcome of a 25-year conservation effortJust inland of Avila Beach, Wild Cherry Canyon is an undeveloped sweep of coastal hills and canyons overlooking San Luis Obispo Bay. Part of the 12,000-acre Diablo Canyon Lands, the property has remained vulnerable to residential development under a long-term private lease. Efforts to protect Wild Cherry Canyon have been under way for more than two decades; however, they have faced several setbacks over the years.Amy Hutzel, Executive Officer of the State Coastal Conservancy, underscored how long this battle had consumed resources and political will. “The Coastal Conservancy and many others have been working to acquire this spectacular piece of the California coast for over 20 years. This large stretch of coastal land offers rare and unique opportunities for habitat conservation, cultural resource protection, and public access. Today we are finally delivering the long-sought protection of this special place,” she said.California’s grant will help acquire both the leasehold and underlying fee title. The acquisition represents far more than a real estate transaction. Wild Cherry Canyon’s coastal prairie, oak woodlands, chaparral, riparian habitat and headwater streams support diverse wildlife. “Conserving an intact coastal landscape at this scale, bolstering protection for the larger Diablo Canyon landscape, and ultimately providing thoughtful public access is the central focus of Wildlands’ mission and core values,” Frazier Haney, Executive Director of The Wildlands Conservancy, said.“Wild Cherry Canyon captures so much of what is special about San Luis Obispo County,” Kaila Dettman, Executive Director of The Land Conservancy of San Luis Obispo County, a potential partner on a future conservation easement for the property, said. “The Irish Hills, with steep oak-studded hillsides, significant biodiversity, and remarkable scenery, have been a key focus of land conservation efforts for decades. To have permanent protection of Wild Cherry Canyon within reach is incredibly meaningful for our community and for everyone who has worked so hard to get us here.”What’s next?Plans are already under way for conservation and public and Tribal use at Wild Cherry Canyon. The Coastal Conservancy and The Wildlands Conservancy will work with the local communities and tribes to develop plans for the same.This conservation also carries profound cultural weight for the Chumash tribes, with ancestral ties to this area. “Wild Cherry Canyon is a special and spiritual place to our Tribe. It’s a place we love and in our terms we belong to it,” Mona Olivas Tucker, Chair of yak titʸu titʸu yak tiłhini tiłhini Northern Chumash Tribe San Luis Obispo County and Region, said. “Our responsibility to care for Wild Cherry Canyon never ends. We’re happy that it will be conserved and look forward to working with The Wildlands Conservancy and Land Conservancy of San Luis Obispo County for the safe keeping of this remarkable place.”A coastal trail on the cards?Along with the conservation efforts, public access is also planned, although visitors will not be able to enter the preserve immediately. A potential five-mile segment of the California Coastal Trail is also on the cards. If implemented, it could eventually form part of a 20-mile route connecting Avila Beach to Montaña de Oro State Park. The authorities are also planning low-impact camping and outdoor education programmes for schools and youth organisations.“For Wildlands, acquisition is the beginning of our responsibility to this land. We look forward to restoring and rewilding the landscape, working with Tribes to support their access and stewardship interests, and creating thoughtful, free public access so people can experience the beauty of Wild Cherry Canyon,” Haney said.Meanwhile, Wild Cherry Canyon is part of the wider Diablo Canyon Lands Conservation Planning Project, which also includes North Ranch and South Ranch near the Diablo Canyon Power Plant.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Google cofounder Larry Page’s wife, a Stanford-trained scientist, has built an ocean-tech organisation; company has donated $120 million-plus in science projects
articles.summary: Tech News News: Around the world, ultra-wealthy individuals and institutions are pouring massive fortunes into projects designed to heal the planet. One of them is Lu.
articles.body: Around the world, ultra-wealthy individuals and institutions are pouring massive fortunes into projects designed to heal the planet. One of them is Lucinda Southworth, wife of Google co-founder Larry Page, a Stanford-trained scientist and one of the most prolific backers of high-tech ocean conservation. Her organisation, Oceankind, is one of the private funding networks for marine science and ecological innovation. It has been reported that the marine-saving powerhouse has donated over $120 million since it was founded in 2018.What Oceankind targets and financesOceankind focuses its financial muscle on marine health and the economic well-being of communities dependent on the sea. According to the website, the group’s operations include conservation, climate-ocean solutions and intersecting environmental priorities, backed through two core strategies: standard policy-advocacy grants and a dedicated Labs Initiative financing early-stage conservation technology.“Our team leverages experience in innovation and environmental philanthropy to promote the development of policies, organisations, and technologies that can scale to help solve the enormous challenges facing the ocean. Of the many issues affecting the marine environment today, we believe that climate change, overfishing, habitat loss, and pollution are the most significant,” it says.According to a 2022 report by TechCrunch, the organisation has donated over $120 million in hidden grants. Notably, as the initiative does not list exact award figures, its financial scale has emerged strictly through investigative reporting by the publication, and since the data is until May 2022, it is highly likely that Oceankind has already poured more than $121 million into environmental programs. Here are the reported disbursements from that period.$18.2 million awarded to ClimateWorks to tackle commercial shipping emissions and carbon capture solutions.Roughly $2 million channeled to Queensland University of Technology to build autonomous coral-reseeding robotics.$1 million directed to the Great Barrier Reef Foundation.$100,000 provided to SkyTruth, enabling its Cerulean system to track 187 maritime vessels tied to intentional oil dumping in its inaugural year.Sector studies later cited by the Chronicle of Philanthropy revealed that those historical figures placed Oceankind as the second-largest private marine benefactor globally, trailing only the Packard Foundation. The broader sector has expanded rapidly, growing from 11 entities donating at least $5 million annually in 2010 to 38 groups by 2022.Unlike traditional American charitable foundations, which must submit open annual tax filings accessible to the public, Oceankind operates under a different corporate structure. The entity is registered in California as a limited liability company, exempting it from the disclosure rules governing conventional non-profit endowments. State business filings (via TechCrunch) indicate that the organisation is administered through the family office handling Page’s personal holdings, while Oceankind has confirmed that Southworth directly supplies its funding.Who is Lucinda SouthworthLucinda Southworth completed her undergraduate studies at the University of Pennsylvania in 2001, earned a master’s degree from Oxford and later submitted her doctoral dissertation in biomedical informatics at Stanford University in December 2008. She married Larry Page on Richard Branson’s Necker Island in December 2007.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Meet the 13-year-old boy with a 168 IQ who will soon pursue a master's at New York University, even before he can drive
articles.summary: US News: At 13, most teenagers are school goers. Joe Petraro-Hyppolite, a teenager from Long Island, New York, is preparing for a very different academic miles.
articles.body: At 13, most teenagers are school goers. Joe Petraro-Hyppolite, a teenager from Long Island, New York, is preparing for a very different academic milestone. He is set to begin a master's program at New York University next fall, according to a report by CBS News. Joe has already earned a high school diploma, completed university-level studies and scored 1,590 on the SAT at the age of 10. His next step will take him into graduate education, where he expects to study sports management, along with kinesiology and biology. If he completes his master's as planned, he could graduate at around the same age that many teenagers are preparing to legally drive a car.From a 1,590 SAT score at 10 to a master's at 13Joe's academic record has attracted attention because of how early he reached milestones that usually come much later. According to CBS News New York, he scored 1,590 on the SAT when he was just 10 years old. At 11, he earned his high school diploma. He then continued his education at Louisiana State University (LSU), where he has been working towards his undergraduate degree. Now, at 13, he has been accepted into a master's program at NYU. "My master's is going to be sports management but other than \(that\) it's also kinesiology and biology," Joe told CBS News New York.He is expected to begin the program next fall, after completing his undergraduate degree. He plans to finish his bachelor's in May next year. The typical age of a person starting a master's program in the US is 33, according to the figures cited in the CBS News New York report. Joe will be less than half that age when he begins his graduate studies.“My IQ is 168”During an interview with CBS News New York, Joe spoke about his IQ and the attention his academic achievements bring. "My IQ is 168," he said. "So you're considered a genius," the reporter replied. "I am not biased, but, yeah, if you say so," Joe said. He also described the comparisons people make when they hear about his achievements."Whenever I tell people, it's like, 'Oh, Young Sheldon, Doogie Howser,'" he said, referring to the fictional young characters known for their exceptional intelligence. Joe's age also stands out when he attends university. He said older students sometimes look twice when they realise how young he is.His mother says every achievement feels surrealJoe's academic journey has also included challenges. According to CBS News New York, he was diagnosed with Tourette syndrome and was once placed in special education classes. His mother, Anne Petraro-Hyppolite, said his progress has been difficult to put into words. "It's just surreal. When he graduated high school so young, it was surreal, but this is ... everything he does is surreal," she said. "He just loves to learn. He is like a sponge."“Who wouldn't be nervous?” Joe on starting at NYUDespite his achievements, Joe does not describe the next stage of his education as something that will necessarily be easy. When asked whether he felt nervous about beginning his master's, he acknowledged the challenge. "Yeah, I mean, who wouldn't be? But then again, I am also excited, because new doors are opening," he said. His planned master's will focus on sports management, while he also intends to study kinesiology and biology. These subjects connect with his wider academic interests and his plans for the future.Joe has said he eventually wants to pursue paleontology. For now, however, his immediate goal is to complete his undergraduate degree before moving on to graduate school. If he follows his current plan, Joe will begin his master's next fall and finish it around the time he reaches the legal driving age.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Archbishop withdraws award to Muslim cleric who called Osama bin Laden 'Muslim warrior'
articles.summary: Europe News: The office of the Archbishop of Canterbury has withdrawn an interfaith award given to Pakistani Muslim cleric Hafiz Muhammad Tahir Mehmood Ashrafi, af.
articles.body: The office of the Archbishop of Canterbury has withdrawn an interfaith award given to Pakistani Muslim cleric Hafiz Muhammad Tahir Mehmood Ashrafi, after earlier comments in which he praised Al-Qaeda founder Osama bin Laden resurfaced. The office said Thursday that it was 'urgently reviewing' the award.Ashrafi received the award from Archbishop Sarah Mullally for “his outstanding work as an ambassador of interfaith harmony in Pakistan”. The presentation took place on September 11, coinciding with the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks in the United States.Lambeth Palace said in a statement sent to AFP, “We are aware of comments circulating online attributed to Hafiz Tahir Ashrafi and we are urgently reviewing this matter.”Ashrafi, chairman of the Pakistan Ulema Council, had told AFP in 2007 that his organisation was giving bin Laden its “highest title for a Muslim warrior” in protest against Britain awarding author Salman Rushdie a knighthood.“We are pleased to award the title of Saifullah (Sword of Allah) to Osama bin Laden,” Ashrafi told AFP at the time, calling this “the highest title for a Muslim warrior”.Bin Laden orchestrated the September 11, 2001 attacks in the US, which killed nearly 3,000 people, and was killed by US forces in Pakistan in 2011.A spokesperson for Ashrafi said his remarks had not been “an endorsement of bin Laden” but were “made in the context of explaining the hurt felt by many Muslims over the British honour” for Rushdie.The spokesperson also stressed Ashrafi's “longstanding record against terrorism and violent extremism”.The comments have since drawn criticism in Britain. Conservative opposition politician Nick Timothy wrote on X, “The naivety of our public institutions for engaging with people like this is staggering. But not surprising.”Rushdie was targeted by fatwas calling for his execution and survived an assassination attempt in 2022 after controversy surrounding his 1988 novel The Satanic Verses.The Church of England is now reviewing the circumstances surrounding Ashrafi’s recognitionCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Google, Bill Gates's fund invests $31.8M in California startup aiming to build solar farm using robots and much less land
articles.summary: US News: Solar plants are currently being touted as the future bitcoins for economies and the environment. As futuristic as the approach towards them may be, t.
articles.body: Solar plants are currently being touted as the future bitcoins for economies and the environment. As futuristic as the approach towards them may be, they still rely on a process that is extremely traditional. Teams arrive at the site, move structures and install thousands of components to make up a structure that can span hundreds of acres. According to an article published by PowerMag, while panels have become cheaper and more efficient, the way they are installed continues to be plagued by labour, land, steel and time bottlenecks.This is a gap that a California-based startup is aiming to fill. Planted just raised $31.8 million to expand a fleet of robots that work directly on solar park installation and launch a new generation of machines called Sage. What has made the buzz, apart from the robotic aspect, is the interest of people in the project: Piva Capital and RA Capital Management Planetary Health led the investment, while Google, Breakthrough Energy Ventures, Khosla Ventures, and Gigascale Capital also participated.Google and a fund created by Bill Gates invested in the company as the competition shifted from merely producing the cheapest panels to identifying those who can convert vacant land into MW faster. Breakthrough Energy Ventures was born from Bill Gates’ initiative to fund climate technologies. Meanwhile, Gigascale Capital was founded by Mike Schroepfer, a former executive at Meta. At the same time, Google’s involvement stands out during a period of rapidly growing electric demand associated with digital infrastructure.This funding comes at a time when the company claims that demand for the robots already exceeds its current capacity. After deploying more than 10MW in 2025, the company stated it aims for 100MW this year, a tenfold increase within a year. Furthermore, its potential project pipeline has already surpassed 20 GW.How it worksInterestingly, the most catching aspect of this project is not the replacement of human labour with robots. Planted is attempting to transform the entire construction process of a solar plant into something of a production line, with software, photovoltaic structures and field robotics to reduce stages that currently take up months or even years.Instead of treating every solar plant as an individual project, the company aims to turn deployment into a repeatable process. It wants software and robots to take up tasks that, as of now, require large teams in the field. The company has developed an integrated system that combines software planning, high-density solar structures that follow the topography, field storage, and robotics.A typical solar farm uses long racks to hold rows of panels that move to track the sun throughout the day, squeezing the maximum amount of power out of each panel. But the design requires flattening the land to accommodate the racks, adding time and expense. The hillier parts of a site might not be used at all. Instead, Planted uses a separate post for each panel, so it can follow the natural terrain without changes. First, the company uses software to build a digital twin—a live virtual model—of the site and plan where each post should go. Then, it uses robots to precisely place each post, pulling them from a compartment that the startup compares to a giant toothpick dispenser. A custom bracket on top makes it possible to snap on a solar panel like putting together a Lego set.The level of precision needed for each post would be difficult to achieve manually. “Placing thousands of foundations precisely is exactly the kind of work that’s slow and error-prone for crews,” said Eric Brown, Planted’s CEO. By following the bumps and hills of the terrain, Planted can pack in more solar panels and build in places that conventional designs couldn’t use.As such, the park is designed with automation in mind from the start. The structure itself has been simplified and prepared for automated installation. Furthermore, the software plays a crucial role in configuring the project. Consequently, the company aims to eliminate steps that typically require manual adjustments during construction.According to the company, its structures are better able to navigate the irregularities of the terrain. As a result, areas that would be problematic for traditional solar trackers can accommodate panels. At the same time, Planted claims to be able to produce twice as much energy per acre, reducing the area occupied by the project.By building directly on the existing landscape instead of grading the land to flatten it, it can also make it easier to get environmental approvals. “How you design a system is pretty related to how you can get it permitted and interconnected,” Brown says. Vegetation stays in place, and stormwater flows the way it did before. The panels also sit lower, so there’s less visual impact on the surrounding area.On the way to successPlanted cites a recent project of 28MW, installed behind the metre to serve a neocloud type data centre. According to the company, 10 months passed from the first contact to the power delivery. Even more impressively, the actual construction in the field took less than three months. The California-based company also pointed to smaller projects that add other advantages. It completed the Bowes Solar project, an 11 MW venture in Illinois for Cultivate Power, while another project managed to reduce its footprint by 10 acres after the original design was rejected by local authorities. In addition, it is preparing the Armoracia project, backed by Aligned Climate Capital.At its core, what the company is selling is speed and in this field, it matters. With the new funding, the startup plans to expand its robotic fleet. It will use part of the resources to launch the Sage, its next-generation robot, in 2026.This transformation occurs in a market where the combination of generation and energy storage is starting to gain increasingly larger projects, such as the Chilean park of 165 MWp paired with a battery that could reach 925 MWh.Overall, solar power is already the dominant new source of energy in the U.S. In the first half of 2026, solar and battery storage made up 70% of new capacity added to the grid. In the second quarter, 9.6 GW of utility-scale solar was installed, up 61% over the same period last year.Brown believes Planted’s approach could help solar grow even faster. “We can see a lot of the cards unfolding where legacy solar wouldn’t be able to meet the moment without some pretty meaningful changes to actually shift from doing hundreds of gigawatts to doing the terawatts that are needed right now,” he says.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A Pennsylvania teacher preserved his family’s white pumpkin for nearly 40 years; the Thanksgiving heirloom is now grown by gardeners
articles.summary: US News: A Pennsylvania teacher helped preserve a family pumpkin that might otherwise have disappeared, growing and stewarding the heirloom for nearly 40 years.
articles.body: A Pennsylvania teacher helped preserve a family pumpkin that might otherwise have disappeared, growing and stewarding the heirloom for nearly 40 years. Wayne Fortna became the caretaker of what is now known as the ‘Fortna White’ pumpkin, a distinctive cream-coloured squash traditionally used to make pumpkin pie for Thanksgiving. After serving as a tank commander under General George S. Patton during the Second World War, Fortna found comfort in gardening and continued growing the family variety for decades. After he died in 1990, his daughter helped save the seeds through the Landis Valley Village and Farm Museum. Today, Seed Savers Exchange shares its seeds with gardeners.How did Wayne Fortna preserve the White pumpkinAccording to the Seed Savers Exchange, before becoming known for preserving the family pumpkin, Fortna served during the Second World War as a tank commander under General George S. Patton. He was a teacher, and he served during the war before returning to civilian life. The organisation says that gardening later became an important source of comfort for him.According to his daughter, Sue Ellen Majer, gardening helped her father cope with the post-war effects of PTSD. She said he found “solace in gardening”, adding that it calmed his nerves and helped reconnect him with nature and the soil. His dedication to growing the family pumpkin therefore became more than simply maintaining a vegetable garden: it was also connected to a deeply personal part of his life after the war.How did Fortna White reach gardenersFortna continued stewarding the family heirloom for almost 40 years, ensuring its seeds could be planted again and that his family could continue enjoying pumpkin pie made from their own squash. The tradition was closely tied to Thanksgiving, when the pumpkin became part of the family's dinner. Its mild flavour and baking qualities made it especially well suited to pie.After Fortna died in 1990, his daughter Sue Ellen sought help from the Landis Valley Village and Farm Museum in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, to preserve the family's treasured seeds. The museum's Heirloom Seed Project has more than 50 volunteers who maintain a collection of historic Pennsylvania Dutch seeds, including the ‘Fortna White’ pumpkin. This intervention helped ensure that the variety survived beyond the Fortna family's own garden.How did Seed Savers Exchange preserve the heirloomSeed Savers Exchange later received ‘Fortna White’ pumpkin seeds from Landis Valley and evaluated the variety through its Collection-to-Catalog pipeline. The organisation ultimately decided that the squash was worth sharing more widely, introducing it as a featured “From the Collection” variety in its 2024 catalogue. Today, gardeners can grow the same heirloom that Fortna carefully maintained for his family for decades. The variety is well suited to pumpkin pies and other dishes.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: US border agents can search any traveler's phone or laptop without a warrant; judges say it's like checking suitcases
articles.summary: US News: Border agents do not require a search warrant to stop a traveler and go through their electronic items like phones and laptops, an appeals court panel.
articles.body: Border agents do not require a search warrant to stop a traveler and go through their electronic items like phones and laptops, an appeals court panel has now ruled. They said the First Amendment does not create a separate requirement that officers obtain a warrant before examining information on a person's phone.The case was brought by Chinwendu Alisigwe, a Green Card holder, whose phone was searched at John F Kennedy International Airport in New York City. He was later convicted of bank fraud and money laundering and it was those border agents who found evidence on his phone.Why the court allowed the phone searchThe court treated a manual search of a cellphone as a routine border search. Under the longstanding border-search exception, government officials generally have broad authority to inspect people and belongings entering the United States without obtaining a warrant.The judges rejected the argument that a cellphone should receive special constitutional protection simply because it contains substantially more personal information than conventional belongings such as luggage or notebooks.The ruling also distinguished border searches from ordinary police searches inside the US. In its 2014 decision in Riley v California, the US Supreme Court generally required police to obtain a warrant before searching the contents of a cellphone seized during an arrest. The Second Circuit concluded that this rule does not apply in the same way at the international border.What about the First Amendment?The case also raised concerns under the First Amendment because phones can contain journalists' work, private messages, political views, photographs and information about a person's professional and personal associations.The Second Circuit nevertheless rejected the argument that the First Amendment creates a separate warrant requirement for cellphone searches at the border.The court noted that phones can contain both constitutionally protected expression and information that does not receive First Amendment protection. It also pointed to the government's authority to enforce immigration and border laws, including restrictions involving certain forms of extremist or terrorist-related expression.What does this mean for travellers?For people entering the US, the ruling means that a border officer does not necessarily need to show evidence of wrongdoing before conducting a manual search of a cellphone.That can potentially affect US citizens, Green Card holders, foreign visitors, students, business travellers and others crossing the US border.Civil liberties groups have warned that the ruling leaves highly sensitive personal information accessible to border officials without any suspicion requirement. The Knight First Amendment Institute, which participated in the case, said the decision could have implications for freedom of speech, association and the press.Not all phone searches are covered by the rulingAn important distinction is that the court ruled on manual searches, such as an officer scrolling through information stored on a phone.It did not resolve all questions surrounding more intrusive forensic searches, in which specialised tools can extract and copy large amounts of data from a device.Other US appeals courts have also drawn a distinction between manual and forensic searches. In July 2026, the Fourth Circuit ruled that manual cellphone searches at the border are routine searches that do not require individualized suspicion, while treating forensic searches differently.The Second Circuit's ruling therefore does not mean that every possible form of digital search at the US border has been definitively cleared of constitutional restrictions.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Pakistan pledges full committment to defence of Saudi Arabia
articles.summary: Assurance comes amid questions over Pakistan and Turkiye’s stance on Riyadh’s fight with Houthis following defence pact.
articles.body:
A senior officer from Pakistan’s military has pledged that his country will defend Saudi Arabia against aggression “to any extent”.

Lieutenant-General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, director-general of the Pakistani military’s media wing, told the Saudi newspaper Arab News on Thursday that Islamabad stands with Saudi Arabia diplomatically and physically.

The promise comes as questions swirl about the stance of Pakistan and Turkiye – both of which signed defence pacts with Riyadh recently – as Yemen’s Houthis intensify their attacks on Saudi Arabia.

“I would like to underscore here the word ‘physically’,” Chaudhry said. “We will go to any extent.”

Pakistani forces are already deployed to protect the kingdom and Islam’s two holiest sites, in Mecca and Medina, he added.

“We are there to protect them, and we will go to any extent further as required by the Saudi leadership and the people of Saudi Arabia.”

However, he did not say whether Riyadh had requested more Pakistani troops or direct involvement against the Houthis.

The Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement, signed by Riyadh and Islamabad in September 2025, says that aggression committed against either country would be regarded as an attack on both.

Invoking this bilateral agreement, Pakistan deployed fighter and support aircraft to Saudi’s King Abdulaziz Air Base in April, after the kingdom came under attack by Iran and its allies.

Alongside Turkiye, the pair then signed off on a mutual defence pact as part of the Mecca Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement last month. However, the pact has yet to be made operational.

Unprovoked aggression against Saudi Arabia, or a spillover of the Yemen conflict into the kingdom, would trigger the pact, Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said earlier this month, but he did not share specific details.

While neither agreement’s full operational provisions have been made public, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has said the Mecca pact works like NATO’s collective defence clause , with the country under attack requesting help from its treaty allies.

However, Pakistan and Turkiye are also anxious to remain mediators in the conflicts roiling the Middle East, and are therefore believed to be unenthusiastic about direct involvement in hostilities.

Chaudhry also stressed that Pakistan continues to work with regional partners towards “a negotiated, peaceful outcome” to the regional crisis triggered by the United States and Israel war on Iran.

Escalating attacks on Saudi Arabia by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi rebel group are putting these pacts to the test.

Pakistan’s Foreign Office said last week that no military response was under discussion under the agreement at the moment, adding that Islamabad would act “when time comes”.

Earlier this week, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said it intercepted a Houthi drone heading towards Mecca , inflaming religious sentiments and drawing a fiery condemnation from Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. On Thursday, Houthi leader Abdel-Malik al-Houthi denied targeting the city, calling it a “heinous lie”.

Islamabad maintains diplomatic channels with Iran , which backs the Houthis.

For their part, the Houthis say they will stay on their current course.

On Friday, the group said Saudi Arabia had carried out about 37 air strikes across Yemen in recent hours, promising to respond by “striking deep inside Saudi territory”.

Al Jazeera’s Nabil al-Yousefi, in Sanaa, reported that Houthi authorities have said the strikes targeted al-Jawf, Saada, Hajjah, Taiz and Lahj governorates, killing five people, three of them children.

The strikes also allegedly targeted telecommunications towers in several localities and were carried out by jets launched from Saudi airbases, Yousefi cites local sources as saying.

In response, the Houthis said they would keep hitting Saudi bases, naming King Khalid Air Base and King Fahd Air Base, in particular.

An overnight attack on the latter resulted in damage to an Italian fighter jet, Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto said.

The Houthis also said they would target “oil companies far away from the holy sites”, Yousefi reported.
