articles.title: Russian hybrid attacks against Europe intensifying, says Macron
articles.summary: The French president says he has tasked the government with protecting critical infrastructure and defence industry sites.
articles.body:
French President Emmanuel Macron has warned that the threat of hybrid attacks by Russia against Europe and France has intensified.

In a news conference at the Elysee Palace, Macron said he had ordered a plan to protect critical infrastructure and defence industry sites in the face of this threat.

He said France had been targeted by Russian hybrid attacks in the past few weeks which would not be left "without a response".

A growing number of European leaders have warned that Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine.

War may be coming. Are we psychologically ready?

Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyberattacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary.

These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary.

The French president was speaking to journalists after meeting party leaders to discuss the security impact of the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine.

Macron mentioned last month's drone attack on Leipzig airport in Germany , blamed on Russia, and remarks by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk suggesting Russia was planning drone and missile strikes against Poland and other countries on Nato's eastern flank.

"In recent weeks, the Russian hybrid threat against Europeans and against France has intensified," he said.

"The intent is to intimidate us and break our effort to support Ukraine. The result will be the exact opposite. We are not intimidated because we know that our security today and tomorrow is at stake in Ukraine."

On Thursday Tusk told Polish MPs that Russian plans included strikes by drones and missiles on countries supporting Ukraine. He said there was a "real risk" of such strikes on the territory of Nato countries, with Moscow then claiming that they were "accidental", in an attempt to split the alliance.

Last Sunday, a Russian drone hit a passenger train near the Ukraine-Poland border shortly after former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson and top European security officials had passed through along the same line.

Ukraine said all the passengers had been evacuated just minutes before the strike at Yahodyn, which hit the train's engine.

There have also been a number of suspicious fires at defence facilities from Italy to Estonia, with some of the affected countries blaming Russia .

Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly said Russia does not plan to attack Europe, but Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov warned European nations against sending troops to Ukraine, which would be seen by Russia as a declaration of war.

"If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war, and it will be very short," he said.

Meanwhile on Friday, Russia reiterated its warning to the UK that any British military facilities in Ukraine used to strike Russian territory were "legitimate targets".

It reserved the right to take "necessary counter-measures" in response to the UK's "fiercely confrontational stance regarding Ukraine", referring to its supply of drones and other weapon systems to Kyiv.

Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Macron also addressed the energy situation, saying that the government had been tasked with protecting critical infrastructure and the "most sensitive" defence industry and technology sites against drone and cyberattacks.

He also announced that France would call a meeting of the G7 to discuss energy and raise the question of gas stocks with the European Commission.

"In the coming weeks, we will have a G7 meeting devoted to these energy issues, both to strengthen cooperation and to avoid unnecessary tensions between the G7 countries and our main partners," Macron said.

"It will also be an opportunity to consider options for a possible release or unlocking of strategic reserves."

articles.title: US voter opposition to war on Iran grows to new highs: Poll
articles.summary: Poll reveals 71 percent in US believe Trump’s team lacks a clear strategy for resolving the conflict.
articles.body:
A new survey has found that a record number of registered voters in the United States oppose the war on Iran and believe there is no strategy to end it.

A survey published on Thursday by Fox News found that 71 percent of voters believe the Trump administration “lacks a clear strategy” for ending the hostilities, which have helped to raise inflation and send fuel prices soaring.

The publication of the poll comes the day before the start of in-person voting for the US midterm elections in November, with the unpopular war helping to send the disapproval rating of President Donald Trump’s overall performance to 61 percent.

Conducted in mid-September, the survey also found that a new high of more than 60 percent of voters believe the US taking military action against Iran was the “wrong decision”.

The poll also found growing concern about the war’s impact on US security. Forty-seven percent of registered voters said the conflict would make the US less safe long term, up from 39 percent in April. Just 32 percent said it would make the country safer.

Early voting in the mid-terms will last six weeks. The election will include votes for the US House of Representatives and the Senate. If the Democrats secure a majority in Congress, they could alter the trajectory of Trump’s final two years as president.

Facing that challenge, Trump has tried to alter voting practices and reshape how US elections are run . He tried to restrict mail ballots, started a pressure campaign to force election officials to share sensitive voter data and initiated an expansive federal investigation into non-citizen voters .

Additionally, the controversial Republican leader has promised a $5,000 payout for every adult US citizen if the party keeps control of both houses.

articles.title: Trump may have breathed new life into the World Trade Organization
articles.summary: The WTO should shift from originating trade agreements to aggregating agreements negotiated elsewhere.
articles.body:
President Trump once called the World Trade Organization “a total disaster.” He may now be giving it a reason to matter again.

Trump’s tariffs are raising the cost of economic dependence on the United States, encouraging trading partners to build alternatives with one another. Canada is explicit about diversifying its trade and is pursuing deeper economic integration with Europe. Australia says it is watching Canada closely while pursuing diversification of its own.

That creates a problem. If countries respond to American unpredictability by constructing their own networks of preferred suppliers, critical minerals partnerships, digital agreements and security relationships, the result could be a more fragmented global economy.

That is not just a threat to the World Trade Organization; it is an opportunity to reinvent it. It should shift from originating trade agreements to aggregating agreements negotiated elsewhere. Canada and Europe show why.

Canada and the European Union already have a Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement . Now they are contemplating deeper integration piece by piece. European Commission President Von der Leyen has proposed an “Alliance for the Future” encompassing technology, defense production, energy, critical minerals, batteries, artificial intelligence and economic security.

This is not a new comprehensive trade agreement. It is integration à la carte. Canada does not have to settle agricultural disputes before integrating defense procurement. Critical minerals cooperation need not await a grand bargain on services. Countries can negotiate where agreement is possible and leave harder issues for later.

Now imagine that Australia, Japan and others do the same. Canada and Europe develop one critical minerals arrangement. Australia negotiates another and Japan creates a third. Governments adopt different digital rules, procurement preferences and supply-chain requirements.

Here, resilience becomes fragmentation. Indeed, the most recent World Trade Report says that targeted agreements in areas such as digital trade and critical minerals can serve as laboratories for deeper cooperation. But they can also fragment trade if they substitute for multilateral rules rather than reinforce them.

The World Trade Organization should embrace the laboratories and aggregate the experiments. Suppose Canada and Europe work out useful rules for critical minerals, and then Australia and Japan want in. Rather than create a spaghetti bowl of bilateral deals, the organization could provide an institutional framework for connecting them though common definitions, transparency, accession procedures and compatible rules.

Aggregation need not mean unconditional most favored nation treatment on every new agreement. The World Trade Organization already offers different models.

The Information Technology Agreement began with 29 participants and expanded to economies accounting for roughly 97 percent of world trade in information technology products. Its tariff concessions are applied on a most favored nation basis, spreading benefits beyond the countries that negotiated them. Participants waited until enough major trading partners were aboard to limit free riding, then extended tariff concessions to all World Trade Organization members. Its research describes critical-mass thresholds historically around 80 percent or more of relevant trade.

The Government Procurement Agreement offers another model in which countries willing to accept common disciplines can join a “plurilateral agreement.” Here, benefits were predicated on reciprocal commitments, with accession available to countries willing to accept the obligations. The agreement is explicitly plurilateral and currently has 22 parties covering 49 members.

The principle should be simple: most favored nation always, reciprocity where necessary and open accession throughout.

Aggregation solves a problem that bilateralism cannot. A Canada-EU agreement may work well for Canada and Europe, but every additional bilateral agreement creates another set of rules for firms and governments to navigate.

The organization can turn replication into expansion: Instead of Australia negotiating its own version of a Canada-EU deal, it can join a common framework. The more countries that join, the more valuable the rules become, and the less incentive there is to create rival ones. Aggregation thus preserves the flexibility of à la carte negotiating without accepting the fragmentation it can produce.

That would give the organization a comparative advantage it badly needs. Instead of trying to originate every new trade rule, it could specialize in aggregation, turning deals negotiated elsewhere into building blocks for a more coherent trading system.

The alternative could be costly. Economists at the World Trade Organization estimate that by 2050, fragmentation into geopolitical blocs could leave global GDP by 5.1 percent below baseline. Replacing multilateral cooperation altogether with a patchwork of free trade agreements could leave it 6.9 percent lower.

Trump’s tariff policies may therefore have created an unexpected opening for an institution he has long criticized. By making dependence on the American market less predictable, they are encouraging countries to construct alternatives. Those alternatives will increasingly originate outside Geneva.

The World Trade Organization does not need to originate the world’s next trade deals. It needs to aggregate the successful ones before their proliferation divides the world economy.

Marc L. Busch is the Karl F. Landegger Professor of International Business Diplomacy at the Walsh School of Foreign Service, Georgetown University. Petros Mavroidis is the Edwin B. Parker Professor of Foreign and Comparative Law at Columbia Law School.

articles.title: The cost of Iran’s regional leverage
articles.summary: Tehran’s use of pressure across the region is putting its rapprochement with Gulf states under increasing strain.
articles.body:
For more than two years, the 2023 Beijing-brokered agreement between Saudi Arabia and Iran seemed to mark a shift in Gulf politics: Away from confrontation and towards managed coexistence. The agreement neither ended strategic rivalry nor sought to do so. Its significance was more limited but still consequential: It created political space for competition to be managed without repeatedly spilling into direct regional escalation. That space came under severe strain earlier this year, when direct Iranian attacks on Saudi Arabia led Riyadh to expel Iran’s military attache and four other embassy staff. Renewed Houthi attacks on Saudi territory and the postponement of planned talks in Oman are now placing what remains of that diplomatic framework under further strain. Together, these developments expose a deeper contradiction at the heart of Tehran’s regional strategy: Can Iran sustain stable diplomatic relations with its Arab Gulf neighbours while continuing to draw strategic leverage from a regional network capable of directly threatening their security?

The attacks: When Yemen’s war crosses the border

The latest escalation marks an important shift in the trajectory of the conflict in Yemen. Fighting that had largely remained within Yemen’s borders has once again crossed into Saudi territory, drawing the consequences of the war directly into the Gulf security environment. On September 8, the Houthis launched a coordinated wave of drone and ballistic missile attacks against several Saudi cities and strategic sites, including Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jizan and Najran.

The significance of this escalation lies not only in the intensity of the attacks but also in their timing and geographic reach. The strikes coincided with renewed fighting between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces around Bab al-Mandeb, one of the region’s most strategically important maritime chokepoints. By mid-September, the escalation had also produced serious humanitarian consequences, displacing tens of thousands of people within Yemen and pushing others across the Red Sea to Djibouti. The Houthi seizure of Mocha and strategic islands around Bab al-Mandeb further underscored the confrontation’s strategic dimension. The conflict, in other words, is no longer defined solely by control of territory within Yemen. It is increasingly tied to control of strategic geography and to the capacity to project pressure beyond Yemen’s borders.

Why now: Hormuz, the Red Sea, and the expanding geography of pressure

The timing matters because the escalation is unfolding alongside growing pressure elsewhere in the region. Since Israel and the United States launched their war on Iran in February, Tehran has severely restricted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, sharply increasing the importance of Saudi Arabia’s western export routes through the Red Sea. That shift has, in turn, increased the strategic importance of Bab al-Mandeb as an alternative gateway for energy flows.

These developments connect two maritime theatres that are often analysed separately. Hormuz is the Gulf’s principal eastern gateway; Bab al-Mandeb provides access to the Red Sea from the west. Simultaneous pressure around both creates a broader geography of strategic vulnerability, extending the consequences of confrontation well beyond the immediate battlefield. In that context, the Houthi position along Yemen’s western coast takes on significance beyond the internal dynamics of the Yemeni conflict. It becomes another point through which pressure can be exerted across the wider regional security system.

The central issue, then, is not whether Tehran directly determines every Houthi military decision. More important is whether developments in Yemen advance or complement Iran’s broader strategic objectives. When pressure around Hormuz coincides with instability around Bab al-Mandeb, two distinct maritime arenas can begin to operate as interconnected sources of leverage. The result is more than an expansion of the conflict itself: It is an expansion of the geography through which strategic pressure can be applied.

The Oman talks: When escalation narrows the space for diplomacy

The postponement of the Oman-hosted talks shows how quickly military escalation can constrict the political space available for diplomacy. Gulf states and Iran had been expected to meet in Salalah to discuss arrangements for managing navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, building on an existing understanding between Tehran and Muscat. The proposed talks were intended to focus on practical maritime security measures, including navigation arrangements and mechanisms for reducing risk around one of the world’s most strategically important waterways.

The regional environment, however, changed faster than the diplomatic process could absorb. Bahrain had already indicated that it would not participate, and Oman subsequently announced the postponement of the meeting, with no new date announced, concluding that the conditions required for productive negotiations were no longer in place. Iran acknowledged that the delay followed concerns raised by some regional states, while reports also pointed to disagreements over elements of the proposed framework.

The importance of the postponement therefore extends beyond the cancellation of a single meeting. It exposes a broader problem for regional diplomacy: Negotiations cannot easily be insulated from the security environment in which they occur. For Saudi Arabia, discussing maritime security with Tehran while simultaneously facing missile and drone attacks from an Iran-aligned actor created an increasingly difficult political contradiction. The question was no longer simply whether dialogue could continue, but whether enough strategic confidence remained for that dialogue to produce meaningful results.

The current escalation therefore raises a broader strategic question: Can Iran continue to extract leverage from regional pressure while preserving its longer-term objective of stable relations with its Arab Gulf neighbours? Since Saudi-Iranian diplomatic relations were restored in 2023, Tehran has sought to present regional dialogue as an alternative to permanent confrontation and to demonstrate that Gulf security can be managed through engagement rather than continual escalation. The durability of that approach, however, depends on more than keeping diplomatic channels open. It also requires convincing neighbouring states that rapprochement can provide a meaningful degree of strategic reassurance.

The current pattern of escalation puts that premise under increasing strain. When missile and drone attacks by an Iran-aligned actor reach Saudi territory at the same time that instability grows around Bab al-Mandeb and Hormuz, Gulf states may find it increasingly difficult to separate their diplomatic relationship with Tehran from their wider security concerns. Again, the decisive issue is not whether Iran directly controls every Houthi decision. Strategically, what matters is the perception that Tehran continues to benefit from a regional network capable of imposing costs on neighbouring states during periods of confrontation.

That dynamic creates a difficult paradox for Tehran. Iran has long sought to prevent the emergence of a more consolidated regional security architecture directed against it. Yet as the geography of pressure widens, Gulf states may have stronger incentives to deepen their external security partnerships and coordinate more closely with one another. An instrument intended to create strategic depth and bargaining leverage can therefore produce the opposite effect: Greater regional coordination around the very security concerns Iran is seeking to contain.

There is, however, another way to interpret Tehran’s calculation. Under direct military pressure and amid growing uncertainty about its regional position, Iran may view pressure generated across multiple fronts as a wartime source of leverage, rather than as the basis of its long-term relations with its neighbours. From that perspective, strategic pressure and regional diplomatic engagement need not be treated as mutually exclusive. They can instead be understood as different phases of the same strategy: Maximise leverage during confrontation, then return to diplomacy once the immediate balance of pressure has shifted.

That calculation carries a substantial strategic risk. It assumes that political trust can be suspended during confrontation and rebuilt afterwards. Yet diplomatic rapprochement involves more than restoring diplomatic representation or reopening channels of communication; its durability depends on expectations about future behaviour. Repeated cycles of escalation followed by diplomatic reset can gradually erode those expectations. Each cycle may therefore make the next attempt at reassurance more difficult and reduce the confidence on which future agreements depend.

The consequences extend beyond Saudi-Iranian relations. China’s role in brokering the 2023 agreement gave the rapprochement a wider international dimension, while the postponement of the Oman talks shows how quickly developments on the ground can narrow the space for regional diplomacy. The more often diplomatic arrangements are overtaken by renewed escalation, the harder it becomes for mediation and regional engagement frameworks to generate durable confidence. The damage is therefore not limited to a single negotiation; it can accumulate across the broader diplomatic architecture intended to contain regional rivalry.

This is ultimately the cost of leverage. Tactical pressure may broaden bargaining options in the short term, but its strategic value becomes harder to sustain when the same pressure begins to weaken the relationships needed for long-term regional stability. For Iran, the central challenge is therefore not simply how much pressure its regional network can generate. It is whether continuing to draw leverage from that network can remain compatible with the regional order Tehran says it wants to build.

articles.title: Europe wants Canada in but keeps Turkey out
articles.summary: Von der Leyen called Canada the “first associate member of the EU,” but Turkey has been an associate member for over six decades.
articles.body:
Earlier this week, in her address on the “the State of the Union,” European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen announced that the EU would invite Canada to join the organization as an Associate Member. Von der Leyen explained that Europe could “no longer rely on [the rules-based system] as the only way to secure our interests” and that it must therefore “build global coalitions for our resilience and democracies.”

She then issued what clearly was intended to be a pointed jab at Washington, and an unambiguous allusion to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s call at the World Economic Forum earlier this year that “Middle powers … act together because if we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu.”

Von der Leyen was not as florid, but she made the same point. “We believe,” she said, “that power does not belong to the strongest, the richest or the loudest, but to all of us … Democracies have the freedom to choose with whom to work.”

For the past eight years Canada and the EU have had a Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement that eliminated 99 per cent of tariffs. Von der Leyen said Europe will move from this agreement to “an Alliance for the Future to create a common prosperity and economic security space.” This more comprehensive cooperative arrangement would include intelligent manufacturing; a new “tech alliance;” integrated defense industrial bases; the Arctic as “a flagship joint project” and joint efforts on energy, critical minerals, batteries, AI, quantum, cyber and economic security.

“In short,” she summarized, “we want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible.” To that end she invited Canada to become the “first associate member of the EU.”

Except that it is not the first. Turkey has been an associate member for over six decades.

The 1963 Ankara Agreement that Turkey and the European Economic Community (the EU’s predecessor) signed in 1963 provided for Turkey’s associate membership . It envisaged a not only the creation of a customs union between them, but the country’s eventual membership in the organization. Seven years later, both sides signed an additional protocol that outlined a long-term schedule for the full implementation of the Customs Union but did not address membership.

The Customs Union finally came into force in 1995. Turkey had applied for membership in 1987, but the European Commission rejected the application two years later. Only in 1999 did the European Union finally agree to give Turkey candidate status. In other words, it accepted the principle that Turkey would someday become an EU member. That day has yet to arrive.

There are numerous reasons the EU has dragged its feet on Turkish membership, starting with concerns about Turkey’s human rights record . For years, Greece also opposed Turkish entry, but it dropped its opposition in 1999.

There continues to be friction over Cyprus, an EU member. Turkey alone recognizes the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, which the United Nations considers a breakaway entity from the Republic of Cyprus. For their part, Turks assert that, in the words of a leading Turkish expert , “the EU created the Greek State of Cyprus.”

There is also popular European opposition to Turkish entry. Turkey’s population of over 85 million swamps that of many EU states — it is equal in size to ten smaller EU members combined.

There is no indication that Turkey will join the EU any time soon. All of the factors that have generated European governments’ and public opposition remain in place. Indeed, the rise of anti-immigration and especially anti-Muslim feeling in much of Europe has only hardened opposition to Turkish entry into the EU.

In contrast, whereas the Canadian government has not yet expressed interest in joining the EU, once it becomes an Associate Member, the door to entry theoretically opens.

As a former British colony and dominion, an independent member of the British Commonwealth, and a founding member of NATO, Canada has always reached out across the Atlantic. Canada’s new arrangement with the EU simply marks another milestone in that long standing relationship. Yet association with the EU is a direct outcome of Canadian friction with the U.S. and Ottawa’s determination both to diversify its international economic relationships and to loosen its ties to what it perceives to be a menacing southern neighbor.

The EU has extended a warm hand to Canada’s recent outreach. Meanwhile, it keeps the door closed to Turkey, despite its longstanding desire for membership, and despite its NATO membership. Sadly, this reflects Europe’s deep-seated fear of forging closer economic and social ties with a powerful and populous Muslim state that is no longer the “ sick man of Europe ” it once was.

Dov S. Zakheim is a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies and vice chairman of the board for the Foreign Policy Research Institute. He was undersecretary of Defense (comptroller) and chief financial officer for the Department of Defense from 2001 to 2004 and a deputy undersecretary of Defense from 1985 to 1987 .

articles.title: ICE to remain without Senate-confirmed chief after White House withdraws Trump’s pick
articles.summary: US News: The White House has withdrawn President Donald Trump’s nomination of former Oklahoma state trooper Lance Schroyer to lead US Immigration and Customs E.
articles.body: The White House has withdrawn President Donald Trump’s nomination of former Oklahoma state trooper Lance Schroyer to lead US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), leaving the agency without a Senate-confirmed director.The withdrawal was announced in a brief notice on Thursday, which did not give a reason for the decision. Schroyer’s nomination had stalled in the Senate after Republican Senator Rand Paul, who chairs the Homeland Security Committee, declined to advance it for a full vote.Paul had sought more information from the White House about the fatal shootings of two US citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, during separate confrontations involving federal immigration agents in Minneapolis in January.Schroyer, who spent 29 years with the Oklahoma Highway Patrol and also served in the US Marines, was serving as a senior adviser to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin when Trump nominated him in June. Mullin, a former Oklahoma senator, is a close ally of Schroyer and oversees ICE through the Department of Homeland Security.Trump had praised Schroyer at the time of his nomination, describing him as a “PATRIOT with real operational experience” and a “proven leader” with decades of law-enforcement experience.However, Schroyer had limited experience specifically in immigration enforcement and had not previously led an agency the size of ICE.ICE has not had a Senate-confirmed director since 2017 and has instead been led by acting chiefs. David Venturella is currently serving as acting director after Todd Lyons left the position in April.The withdrawal means Venturella is expected to continue leading ICE while the administration considers its next nominee. The agency is central to Trump's immigration agenda and his push for a large-scale deportation programme.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Singer-songwriter and Broadway composer Duncan Sheik dies at 56
articles.summary: Singer-songwriter and Broadway composer Duncan Sheik has died, according to a post on his Instagram account.
articles.body: Singer-songwriter and Broadway composer Duncan Sheik has died, according to a post on his Instagram account. He was 56. His mother, Suzanne Sheik, told The New York Times that his cause of death Thursday night was cardiac arrest. “The world has a lost a singular talent, and deeply influential voice in music and theater. From his Grammy-nominated hit ‘Barely Breathing’ to his groundbreaking, Tony and Grammy Award-winning work on Spring Awakening, Duncan’s artistry touched many and leaves an indelible mark on the cultural landscape,” the Instagram statement said. “Duncan was a father, husband, son, brother, and friend. He will be remembered for his sensitivity, wit, inteligence [sic], and depth of spirit he brought to those who knew and loved him,” it continued. “We are deeply grateful for the outpouring of love from his fans, friends, collaborators, and the artistic community,” the statement said. “His musical legacy will continue to inspire generations to come.” “Duncan passed away last night surrounded by love,” the statement added. Sheik had recently been receiving medical care, with his family saying in a statement on Wednesday that he was in “critical but stable condition.” At the time, it was not immediately clear what he was being treated for or where. Sheik shared a daughter with his longtime girlfriend, Nora Ariffin, and was a practicing Buddhist. Sheik exploded onto the pop music scene in 1996 with the hit single “Barely Breathing.” The song earned him a Grammy nomination for best male pop vocal performance. He went on to release nine studio albums over his career, but “Barely Breathing” remains at the top of Sheik’s Spotify page. His most recent album was released in 2022. In 2020, he told HuffPost that he used to resent performing “Barely Breathing” because “it lived on the radio far longer than it should have,” he said. “And then other things that I was hoping would make it onto the radio never got a chance to, so I was being cock-blocked by my own song at the time.” Breaking out on Broadway Sheik also found his footing composing for the theater. His first gig for the stage came in 2002, when he composed the music for the New York Shakespeare Festival production of “Twelfth Night.” Sheik saw his biggest theater break in 2006, when he and Steven Sater wrote the music for the breakout Broadway musical “Spring Awakening,” an adaptation of a German play from the 1800s. The show proved to be a big break for many: Actors Lea Michele and Jonathan Groff got their first major Broadway jobs playing the starring roles. Sheik went on to win two Tony Awards for the “Spring Awakening” music, including best orchestrations and best original score, which he shared with Sater. “Spring Awakening” also won best musical that year at the Tony Awards and earned a Grammy Award for best musical show album. According to a 2012 Broadway World article, Sheik said he had been working on the music for a film adaptation of “Spring Awakening.” It is unclear whether that project is still in the works. The show’s off-Broadway revival, however, is set to begin previews on Nov. 27 and officially open on Dec. 17. Sheik told freelance music journalist Daniel Van Auken that he met Sater through Buddhism. He said it was Sater who pitched turning “Spring Awakening” into a musical. “So, Steven said, ‘Why don’t we adapt this show [Spring Awakening] as a musical?’” Sheik recalled to Van Auken in 2024. “Initially, I was like, ‘It’s a f-----g terrible idea. I don’t want to write a musical!’ But then we did it! And that’s how it went down.” Sheik penned the music for several other shows throughout his career, including “Alice by Heart” (2012), “American Psycho” (2013), “The Taming of the Shrew” (2016) and “The Secret Life of Bees” (2019). Sheik told Billboard in 2016 that writing the music for “American Psycho” “became very exciting and cool to create a piece of musical theater where you had the initial emergence of house music and early techno and then all the things that came out of it.” He said that at first, “the main thing was understanding the world Patrick Bateman was living in and what that music might have sounded like.” Personal life and struggles with alcohol In 2011, Sheik canceled tour dates in support of his album “Cover 80s.” In a since-archived post from Sheik’s Tumblr account, the artist told fans he had been receiving care for alcohol addiction at the time. “While this episode may sound like a low point, the experience actually confirmed for me how much I want to go forward in my creative life, and how much I sincerely value all of those who have supported me,” Sheik wrote in the post. After receiving treatment, Sheik wrote he was working on music for several musical theater projects while spending time in Jakarta, Indonesia. As for Buddhism, Sheik said it made him more comfortable with his life as a performer. He told ABC News in 2016 that a form of mantra meditation, a practice of Nichiren Buddhism, is what helped him conquer his nerves. “I was an incredibly self-conscious performer and singer,” the singer-songwriter told ABC News. “And there was something about chanting where you’re just sitting on one note kind of continually that really taught me how to sing one note. If you know how to sing one note, then possibly you can learn how to sing two notes, and then three, maybe four, and there was something really great about using my voice in this very calm and specific way that helped me a lot in terms of becoming someone who could actually get on stage and sing.” Buddhist themes appeared frequently in the art Sheik created, including in “Spring Awakening,” a show about a group of German teenagers discovering their sexuality in the face of 19th-century repression, he explained. “In Buddhism, there’s this idea that at any given moment you’re kind of shifting through these 10 different life states, so hell, hunger, anomaly, anger, tranquility, rapture, learning, realization … compassion and enlightenment, and at any given moment … you’re inhabiting one of these states,” he said, according to ABC News. “And certainly in ‘Spring Awakening’ you do have all of these life states represented in terms of what happens to these kids and their kind of reaction to it.” In 2024, when asked what he was proudest of in his career, Sheik told Van Auken, the freelance journalist, that it was “the fact that I don’t feel like I have too many things that I’ve released that are embarrassing to me.” “I’ve been able to do what I wanted musically, which feels very gratifying,” Sheik said. “Even very obscure and deep album tracks that probably very few people have heard, I’m really proud of that stuff.”

articles.title: White House TikTok post goes silent after scathing Zara Larsson critique
articles.summary: A White House TikTok video, celebrating ICE-led deportations went silent on Friday after singer Zara Larsson tore into the administration for using her song “Midnight Sun” in the post.
articles.body: A White House TikTok video, celebrating ICE-led deportations went silent on Friday after singer Zara Larsson tore into the administration for using her song “Midnight Sun” in the post. The Swedish artist took to TikTok, flashed an “L” sign with her thumb and index finger and called the White House “losers” for borrowing a tune that celebrates the joy of Scandinavian nature to soundtrack a celebration of mass deportations. “It’s just so f---ing uncool,” she told 12.5 million TikTok followers on Thursday. “You guys are such f---ing losers.” By Friday morning, that video had gone silent displaying the message: “This sound is unavailable.” It wasn’t immediately clear if TikTok had acted to protect Larsson’s work or whether the White House muted the video itself. Representatives for the platform and administration could not be immediately reached for comment on Friday. “If you want to talk about politics and immigration politics, fine,” Larsson said. “But that’s really not what this is. This video is so dehumanizing.” The White House video appeared to show agents arresting men, implying that they were undocumented immigrants. Larsson said she was struck that many of the detained appeared to be wearing neon-colored protective work clothes, the kind common on construction sites or on the highway. “These people in this video, they’re real people. There’s a f---ing guy in there with construction wear,” Larsson said. “He’s working and a vast majority of these people who are undocumented are regular people with jobs. They’re just trying to have a better future. I don’t understand. I don’t understand why you would do this video. ” The 28-year-old Stockholm native said she’s keenly aware of the opportunities afforded to her growing up in Sweden. “I consider myself so lucky with the life that I’ve been dealt. The fact that I’m born in Sweden, I have healthcare, I’ve had an education, I’ve had all these opportunities just laid out in front of me,” the artist said. “I can travel, I get to do all of these amazing things-that’s luck. That’s luck. So much of that is luck, and there, there’s people out there who are who are not that lucky, and they want to have a better life for their families or for themselves and their children.” Larrson has rarely shied away from using her platform to express any number of views. She’s been, for years, highly critical of Chris Brown and his past incidents of domestic violence. “There are so many artists I have blocked on Spotify, and all of them are, like, abusers,” Larsson told Cosmopolitan earlier this year. “You certainly wouldn’t find, like, a Chris Brown song.” Also this year, Larsson said she lost a $3 million brand deal over a dark joke she made to support a fan who revealed she’d gotten an abortion after one of the singer-songwriter’s shows.

articles.title: Pilot’s sudden death during overnight layover puts spotlight on fatigue concerns
articles.summary: An Air India captain, Sunny Sharad Asaldekar, 46, was found unresponsive in his New Delhi hotel room during a layover, sparking renewed fatigue concerns for pilots.
articles.body: An Air India captain was found unresponsive in his hotel room during an overnight flight layover in New Delhi, and was later pronounced dead at a hospital. The captain has been identified as Sunny Sharad Asaldekar, 46, The New Indian Express reported. He had checked into the hotel on Thursday, and his brother contacted the hotel manager the following evening after Asaldekar stopped answering calls. The hotel manager entered the locked room with a master key and found Asaldekar unconscious and unresponsive, according to the outlet. 'WE NEED TO RETURN IMMEDIATELY,' FLIGHT CREW WARNS AS PILOT HEALTH EMERGENCY UNFOLDS Police responded to the hotel, and Asaldekar was taken to a hospital, where he was declared dead. "Air India is deeply saddened at the passing away of a cockpit crew member in Delhi last night," the airline said in a statement to The New Indian Express. "He was on a layover rest at a hotel in Delhi where he was found unconscious last evening. He was rushed to the hospital immediately, where he was declared dead." A post-mortem examination was conducted, but the cause of death has not yet been determined. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The Federation of Indian Pilots renewed its call for an urgent review of fatigue-management practices after the pilot's death but said it was not directly linking fatigue to his death, according to The Times of India. Matthew "Whiz" Buckley, a former U.S. Navy F/A-18 Hornet fighter pilot who also flew for American Airlines and FedEx, told Fox News Digital that fatigue has long been a concern in commercial aviation. "Pilot fatigue in aviation has been an issue since day one," Buckley said. While passengers may assume an overnight layover gives pilots plenty of time to recover, Buckley said required rest does not always mean pilots get enough sleep. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES "A layover is just that. It's a crew laying over in a city that is not their home base," he said. Pilots may arrive at a hotel in the early morning hours and then try to sleep during the day, Buckley said, which can work against the body's natural sleep cycle. "It's just unnatural to sleep during off hours," he said. Buckley said he faced that challenge while flying overnight routes himself — and that pilot fatigue was among the reasons he made changes in his career. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Long-haul flights can be especially difficult when pilots cross multiple time zones, he added. "Where it really takes a toll on the body for pilots is east-west," Buckley said. "When you're crossing multiple time zones, [that's] when your body can really get messed up." Fatigue can also build up beyond one flight or layover, according to Buckley, who cited irregular hours and prolonged periods of sitting, plus diet issues, exercise challenges and time away from family as factors that can affect pilots. Buckley said U.S. safeguards include federal crew-rest requirements, airline policies and labor agreements, but pilots also play a key role in deciding whether they are fit to fly. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "At the end of the day ... you know who determines if a pilot is fit to fly? You," Buckley said. Fox News Digital reached out to Air India for comment.

articles.title: ‘World’s best airline’ for 2026 is named
articles.summary: Qatar Airways drops to second place in the annual Skytrax rankings of the world’s best airlines as an Asian carrier take the crown in tough year for the aviation industry.
articles.body: Wars. Climate chaos. Soaring fuel prices. Disruptive passengers duct-taped to their seats. It’s not getting any easier to run an airline in these turbulent times, but some are clearly doing it better than others. In recognition of that, the annual Skytrax Awards — known as the aviation industry’s Oscars for their glitzy celebration of the global and regional airlines that mostly get us to where we want to go — has once again convened to crown one as the world’s best. For 2026 the winner is Singapore Airlines. The Asian carrier was presented with the award at a ceremony on Friday at London’s posh Langham Hotel, where fiercely competitive airline bosses briefly gathered under a mutual truce for handshakes, canapés and a slew of other trophies recognizing everything from onboard Wi-Fi to cabin cleanliness. It was the sixth time Singapore has picked up the top prize in the awards’ 25-year history, adding to previous wins in 2023, 2018 and a clutch in the noughties. It reclaimed it from last year’s victor, Qatar Airways, which has won nine times in the past 15 years. In fact, as Skytrax CEO Edward Plaisted noted, the award has almost exclusively remained in the possession of an elite cadre of seven airlines, most of which still managed to place in this year’s top 20. Dance routines In the final rundown, Qatar dropped down to second place, with Cathay Pacific Airways, Japan’s All Nippon Airways, Turkish Airlines and Emirates rounding out the top six. Only past winner British Airways was missing from this year’s list. US carriers were completely absent — a frequent state of affairs on the Skytrax list — with Air Canada the sole North American representative. The big prize, said Goh Choon Phong, Singapore’s CEO, in a pre-prepared statement, was a “testament to the dedication and professionalism of our people.” Some of those people were among the many flight crews attending the event in full uniform — a dash of color in a room dominated by dark blue suits. A lucky few got to perform dance routines on stage for the gathered crowd. Singapore also picked up trophies for its economy class and economy class catering. There were plenty of other prizes to go around — all determined by a global customer satisfaction survey organized by Skytrax, a UK-based aviation consultancy. Qatar was named best carrier in the Middle East, and also won prizes for its business class, onboard Wi-Fi and business-class lounge. Cathay Pacific picked up prizes for its cabin crew and first-class airline lounge. All the glad-handing couldn’t quite cast off the numerous shadows facing the aviation industry right now, with the Iran conflict, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the rising cost of oil, new aircraft delays and souring US international relations among the topics discussed on the sidelines. ‘A bit of a bad year’ Perhaps acknowledging a recent UK air traffic meltdown that heavily disrupted flights in and out of the country, the event’s emcee — announcing that one award was being presented early to allow its recipient to dash for a flight departing in under three hours — remarked: “Good luck with that.” Yet, said Skytrax’s Plaisted, the quality being offered by airlines to flyers continues to grow each — even in “a bit of a bad year.” “The passenger experience, mainly driven by the industry’s increasingly fierce competition, is always getting better,” he told CNN. “It takes a big event — a 9/11 event — to really cause a problem.” Other notable awards included recognition of emerging Taiwanese carrier STARLUX’s ascendancy to Skytrax’s five-star rating category. Importantly, in the post-Covid age, it also took home the award for cleanest cabin. Meanwhile, Air France won best first class and EVA Air, another Taiwanese carrier, won best premium economy. The top five budget airlines were named as: AirAsia, Scoot, Vueling, Eurowings and Iberia Express. Bangkok Airways was named best airline in Asia — and best regional airline globally. Ethiopian Airlines was the best in Africa, Chilean multinational carrier LATAM led in South America, while Turkish Airlines was the best in Europe. In North America, Air Canada was declared the winner. It also picked up the trophy for best business class lounge dining. Fight for premium Mark Nasr, Air Canada’s executive vice president, said the Skytrax awards — which come as the airline is looking to expand its role as a global carrier, not just serving routes to and from Canada — are crucial for survival as carriers increasingly look to big spenders to keep them afloat. “The industry is getting more competitive,” he told CNN. “There’s a theme right now around the growth of premium travel and customers that are very discerning. They have large budgets, and airlines are investing to earn that business. With fuel prices increasing so much, the airlines that will be able to sustain themselves will be the ones able to charge a premium to justify their products.” Air Canada was well-placed to survive the current storms thanks to a healthy balance sheet, loyal customer base and resilient staff, Nasr said. The airline will also endure the recent President Trump-fueled spats between Canada and the United States. “Relationships ebb and flow over time, but we continue to believe in the core strength of the partnership — economic and social — between the US and Canada and we’ll weather the current circumstances.” Skytrax’s airlines of the year 2026

articles.title: Uber ordered to pay $40 million to family of US woman killed on California highway
articles.summary: US News: Uber has been ordered to pay $40 million to the parents of a 23-year-old woman who was fatally struck by a vehicle on a California highway after a dri.
articles.body: Uber has been ordered to pay $40 million to the parents of a 23-year-old woman who was fatally struck by a vehicle on a California highway after a driver allegedly forced her and her friend out of the car.According to the BBC, Emily Normandin-Parker had booked an Uber with a friend to get home after a night out on August 12, 2023. During the ride, her friend became sick and vomited inside the car, following which the driver, Vu Tran, pulled over on State Route 73 in Orange County and left the two women on the side of the freeway.Normandin-Parker was then struck and killed by another vehicle as the Uber drove away, according to her family's lawyers. Her parents, Carol Normandin and Ken Parker, said their daughter had made the decision not to drive because she was intoxicated and had trusted Uber to get her home safely.“Emily did everything Uber tells riders to do - she made the responsible choice not to drive and we trusted Uber to get her home safely,” her parents said in a statement. “That trust cost our daughter her life.”The $40 million award was issued following a five-day arbitration process, with retired judge Richard Stone ordering Uber to pay $20 million each to Normandin and Parker.During the proceedings, Uber argued that Tran was an independent contractor and that the company should not be held legally responsible for his actions.The family's lawyers said Tran did not call for help after leaving the women on the highway. Instead, they alleged, he pulled away and contacted Uber to seek a cleaning fee after the vomiting incident.Stone said the driver had shown “far more worry for his new car than he did for his passengers”, and noted that he could have taken an exit and dropped the women at a safe location.Uber said it disagreed with the decision and believed the arbitrator was wrong to hold the company legally responsible.“No family should have to suffer the loss of a child, and our thoughts continue to be with the Normandin-Parker family,” Uber said, adding that it has strengthened its safety measures, including guidance to drivers to avoid dropping passengers at unsafe locations.The family's law firm, Panish Shea Ravipudi LLP, said Uber had initially proposed a settlement that would have paid the parents $10 million but barred them from publicly discussing the incident. The family rejected the proposal.The parents have since established the Emily Normandin-Parker Foundation in their daughter's memory and are advocating for stronger rideshare safety regulations.
